slides.title: Chapter 3: Bitcoin Core
slides.notes: Chapter 2 followed one payment through the network; this chapter opens the program that checks every rule. Point at the three coins and the picture: a coin turning into code. Ask who has ever run software they did not write: every number in this deck was computed by the chapter library from saved data.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.take: Seven parts, three true stories, nineteen examples
slides.notes: The route has seven parts, from the source code to the toolkits around the node. Point at the three counters: slides, true stories and code examples. Tell students every example has a twin on the course page. Ask them to keep one question in mind for each part.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers

items: What makes Bitcoin Core the reference implementation of Bitcoin?
How do I choose a release, check it and build it from source?
Which settings decide what a node stores, remembers and trusts?
How do I ask a running node questions, and who may ask?
How do I decode a transaction and tell its txid from its weight?
How can I check a block myself, and what else can talk to a node?

slides.notes: Read the six questions aloud and promise to return to them in the summary. Ask who can already answer the second one, about choosing and checking a release. A common mistake is to treat the first question as history; it is about what makes a program the reference.

slides.title: The chapter in one picture
slides.take: Six steps from the source code to the data of the chain
slides.notes: This map is the skeleton of the lecture: six steps from source code to the data of the chain. Point at the arrows and ask where in the chain a student would expect to meet the first problem. Most say the build. The nineteen examples run along this path.

slides.title: From Bitcoin to Bitcoin Core
slides.sub: Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation

items.meaning: The program against which other programs are measured.
items.analogy: Think of the standard metre bar that every ruler was checked against.

items.meaning: A node that downloads every block and checks every rule itself.
items.analogy: Think of an auditor who recounts every receipt instead of trusting a summary.

items.meaning: A numbered public document that proposes a change to Bitcoin.
items.analogy: Think of a numbered bylaw proposed in a club's rulebook.

slides.notes: Part 1 asks what Bitcoin Core is. Point at the three tiles and read each comparison aloud. Ask which of the three a student could explain to a friend. A common mistake is to call Bitcoin Core the only possible node: it is the reference, not the only client.

slides.title: Version 0.1, set in stone
slides.sub: 8 January 2009 · the first release of Bitcoin

items.cap: Picture: Satoshi bust, Budapest - Fekist, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, announcing on the metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list

slides.take: The program came first: the reference implementation defines the rules
slides.notes: Tell the story slowly: Satoshi Nakamoto, 8 January 2009, a mailing list, five days after the first block. Point at the bust and at the source link at the bottom. Ask why software had to come before rules. A common mistake is to think the white paper alone defined Bitcoin.

slides.title: Inside the program
slides.take: One program: it listens, checks, stores and answers
slides.notes: Bitcoin Core is one program with parts. Point at the four boxes from top to bottom: connect, validate, store, answer. Ask which part a wallet would call: the RPC part. A common mistake is to picture the node as a database only; the validation engine is its heart.

slides.title: What a full node does all day
slides.sub: Peers, the initial download and checking every rule
slides.notes: A full node follows five steps. Point at the third box: the initial download, where a new node validates the whole chain. Ask how much a node that was off for ten days must fetch: about four gigabytes. A common mistake is to think a node trusts a peer's summary.
slides.take: A full node trusts nobody: it checks every rule itself

slides.title: A version number that carries a vote
slides.sub: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal signals through bit flags
slides.take: Think of a ballot with 29 tick boxes, one for each proposal
slides.notes: A block's version field is not a counter. Point at the orange group, 0010: the top three bits mark the scheme, and bit 1 in the last group is the vote. Ask how many proposals can vote in parallel: twenty-nine bits, so up to twenty-nine at once.

slides.title: Open source and the forks of Bitcoin
slides.sub: Anyone may read the code; a soft fork tightens the rules
slides.notes: Open source means anyone may read, change and share the code under a licence; Core uses MIT. Point at the two nested boxes: a soft fork accepts fewer blocks than before. Ask why old nodes keep following: every new block is valid for them too.
slides.take: A soft fork only tightens the rules, so old nodes still follow the chain

slides.title: Bitcoin Development Environment
slides.sub: Compiling Bitcoin Core from the Source Code

items.meaning: A name that fixes one exact version of the source, such as v31.1.
items.analogy: Think of a bookmark that always opens the same page.

items.meaning: A tagged version offered for testing before it becomes final.
items.analogy: Think of a dress rehearsal before the opening night.

items.meaning: The node program, which runs in the background.
items.analogy: Think of the engine of a car, working while you do other things.

slides.notes: Part 2 turns source code into programs. Point at the three tiles: a tag fixes a version, a candidate is a rehearsal, bitcoind is the node. Ask why a bookmark is a good picture for a tag. A common mistake is to build a release candidate and call it a release.

slides.title: Three steps from source to executables
slides.take: Select, configure, build: three steps, one set of programs
slides.notes: A build has three decisions. Point at the three boxes from left to right and ask which decision changes the result most. Configuring does, because options decide what is built. A common mistake is to skip the tag and build whatever the main branch holds that day.

slides.title: From a git clone to bitcoind
slides.sub: The tools between the source code and the programs
slides.notes: Five steps lead from source to program. Point at the table: the older Autotools commands beside the current CMake ones. Ask why the table has two columns: the book used one, Core now uses the other: the bitcoin command is the front door to the programs.
slides.take: Clone, install the prerequisites, configure, compile

slides.title: Release tags sort by number, not by letters
slides.sub: A release tag names the version; a release candidate carries rc
slides.take: Think of edition numbers: the tenth edition follows the ninth
slides.notes: These are real tags of the Bitcoin repository. Point at the two orders in the table: as text, v0.10.0 comes first; by number, v0.9.5. Ask why text order is wrong: because the character 1 sorts before 9: leave out release candidates first, as the code does.

slides.title: What a release folder holds
slides.sub: bitcoind is the node; bitcoin-cli is the client that calls it
slides.take: Think of bitcoind as the engine and bitcoin-cli as the steering wheel
slides.notes: A release unpacks into seven programs in bin and three helper parts in libexec. Point at bitcoind, the node, and at bitcoin-cli, the client that calls it. Ask which one students would run first. A common mistake is to run bitcoin-cli with no node running.

slides.title: Dozens of builders, one identical binary
slides.sub: 13 September 2021 · Bitcoin Core 22.0 moves to Guix

items.cap: Picture: GNU Guix logo - GNU Guix, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

items.who: Carl Dong, who wrote the Guix build system that Bitcoin Core adopted for release 22.0, and the independent builders who sign its results

slides.take: Verify, don't trust: the project applies its own rule to itself
slides.notes: Tell it as a story: Carl Dong's Guix, release 22.0, 13 September 2021. Point at the logo and the guix.sigs link. Ask why many builders signing the same hash beat one signer. A common mistake is to think a signature proves the code is good: it proves the file matches.

slides.title: A download must match its published hash
slides.sub: Checking a release against SHA256SUMS
slides.take: Think of the safety seal on a medicine bottle: break it and you can tell
slides.notes: Each release ships a list of hashes. Point at the two boxes that must read the same, then at the third: equal. Ask what a single changed bit would do to the hash: it would change completely. A common mistake is to compare only the first characters by eye.

slides.title: Three checks before you trust a download
slides.sub: Checksum, signature and reproducible build
slides.notes: A download is checked three ways. Point at the three columns: checksum, signature, reproducible build. Ask what each one cannot show: a checksum alone cannot show who published it. A common mistake is to think a good signature proves the signer is trustworthy.
slides.take: Each check closes one gap; none proves the signers deserve trust

slides.title: Running a Bitcoin Core Node
slides.sub: Configuring the Bitcoin Core Node

items.meaning: A text file of settings that the node reads when it starts.
items.analogy: Think of the settings card taped to a coffee machine.

items.meaning: The folder in which the node keeps blocks, state, logs and settings.
items.analogy: Think of the node's filing cabinet.

items.meaning: An option that deletes old block files after the node has checked them.
items.analogy: Think of an accountant who audits old invoices, keeps the totals and shreds the paper.

slides.notes: Part 3 starts the node and sets it up. Point at the three tiles: a file of settings, the data directory, pruning. Ask which setting trades disk for features: pruning does. A common mistake is to prune first and ask for the transaction index later.

slides.title: The command line wins over the file
slides.sub: The configuration file sets defaults; an option on the command line overrides them
slides.take: Think of a recipe card that you may override with a note on the fridge
slides.notes: A configuration file holds defaults; the command line overrides them. Point at the line where the file is merged first and the command line last. Ask what the node uses when both set the same option: the command line wins. A common mistake is to reverse the order of the merge.

slides.title: Options and the start-up log
slides.sub: One option can come from three places; the log shows the result
slides.notes: One option can come from three places. Point at the ladder: the command line sits on top and wins. Then point at the start-up log: it is how you see what the node really did. Ask where alertnotify is set: in the configuration; a common mistake is to ignore the log.
slides.take: The command line wins; the log tells you what the node did

slides.title: Inside the data directory
slides.sub: What the offline node of release 31.1 had written
slides.take: The data directory is the whole memory of the node
slides.notes: Everything the node knows lives in its data directory. Point at the largest rows, blocks and chain state, and at the cookie file that exists only while the node runs. Ask which folder is the node's diary: the log. A common mistake is to delete the folder to free space.

slides.title: How the database cache is shared out
slides.sub: The dbcache setting is divided before it is used
slides.take: Think of a desk: two small drawers and one very large tabletop
slides.notes: The dbcache option is divided before it is used. Point at the two tiny bars and the huge one: 2, 8 and 1,014 MiB. Ask where nearly all the memory goes: to the coins cache. A common mistake is to think a bigger dbcache grows every database equally.

slides.title: Pruning and the transaction index do not mix
slides.sub: prune deletes old blocks; txindex needs every block
slides.take: Think of a library that shreds old books and so cannot catalogue them all
slides.notes: Pruning keeps only recent blocks; the transaction index needs every block. Point at the third verdict, refused, and at the recorded refusal of release 31.1. Ask why the two cannot live together: a node cannot index what it has deleted. Students often expect a quiet downgrade.

slides.title: Two ways to spend less memory
slides.sub: The blocksonly and maxmempool options
slides.take: A node can trade features for memory, and keep verifying everything
slides.notes: Two settings reduce what a node asks of its machine. Point at the chart: 286 MiB against about 5 MB in blocks-only mode. Ask what blocks-only gives up: loose transactions, not verification. A common mistake is to think a smaller memory limit means a weaker node.

slides.title: An alert text is cleaned before it runs
slides.sub: The alertnotify option runs your command when the node raises an alert
slides.take: Think of a mail room that removes anything dangerous before a letter reaches you
slides.notes: The node can run a script of yours when something is wrong. Point at the two quotes in the hostile text and at the cleaned text beside them. Ask what the quotes would do in the shell: they would end the word and start a second command: cleaning is the defence.

slides.title: Wallets inside the node: descriptors
slides.sub: How a node describes the scripts it can spend
slides.notes: A descriptor wallet is the current default, stored in SQLite; the legacy wallet can only be migrated. Point at the table of output types and ask which one the store's 75,000 satoshis used: P2WPKH. A common mistake is to think an address and a descriptor are the same thing.
slides.take: A descriptor says in one line what a wallet can watch and spend

slides.title: The project that outlives its keyholders
slides.sub: 7 April 2014 · Andresen hands over to van der Laan

items.cap: Picture: Gavin Andresen, 2014 - Stephen McCarthy, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, Gavin Andresen and Wladimir van der Laan, who passed the lead role of the Bitcoin software on in 2011 and 2014
items.where: the public bitcoin/bitcoin repository on GitHub

slides.take: The reference implementation is an institution, not a person
slides.notes: Tell it as a story: Gavin Andresen hands the lead to Wladimir van der Laan on 7 April 2014. Point at the photograph and the link. Ask who holds the keys today: a team does, reviewing in public. A common mistake is to think one person controls Bitcoin Core.

slides.title: Bitcoin Core API
slides.sub: Getting Information on Bitcoin Core's Status

items.meaning: A command-line tool that calls the node's interface.
items.analogy: Think of a remote control for the node.

items.meaning: A way to call a program's functions with small JSON messages.
items.analogy: Think of an order slip handed over a counter.

items.meaning: A secret that the node writes to a file at every start.
items.analogy: Think of a hotel key card coded anew for each guest.

items.meaning: A stored user name with a salted hash of the password.
items.analogy: Think of a bank that keeps a check value, not your PIN.

slides.notes: Part 4 talks to a running node. Point at the four tiles: the client, the message format, the cookie and the fixed credential. Ask which one a script on the same machine would use: the cookie. A common mistake is to open the interface to the whole internet.

slides.title: An API is a menu of questions
slides.sub: From your program to the node and back, in JSON
slides.notes: An API is a menu of questions a program may ask. Point at the stack: your program, the API, JSON-RPC over HTTP, and the JSON answer. Ask which part bitcoin-cli plays: the client. A common mistake is to think the node speaks a special language: it speaks plain HTTP.
slides.take: You may ask only what the menu offers, and the answer is JSON

slides.title: One JSON-RPC call and its reply
slides.sub: JSON-RPC is how every client talks to the node
slides.take: Think of an order slip: the same fields every time, and an answer on the same slip
slides.notes: A call is a small JSON text with a method; the reply holds a result, an error and the id. Point at the three boxes in a row and at the error: empty means success. Ask what an id is for: it matches the answer to the question.

slides.title: The cookie is a fresh password
slides.sub: Cookie authentication needs no password to invent or store
slides.take: Think of a hotel key card that is recoded for every guest
slides.notes: At every start bitcoind writes a new random secret to the cookie file. Point at the 64 characters and the 32 bytes behind them. Ask why nothing needs to be stored: the secret is new each time. A common mistake is to copy the cookie into scripts.

slides.title: rpcauth stores a salted hash, not the password
slides.sub: A fixed credential for programs that cannot read the cookie
slides.take: Think of a bank that keeps a check value and never your PIN
slides.notes: The rpcauth line holds a user, a salt and a keyed hash of the password. Point at the three lengths: 5, 32 and 64. Ask what a thief gets from the file: only the hash. A common mistake is to think a salt is a second password.

slides.title: Cookie or hashed credentials?
slides.sub: Two ways for a program to prove it may call the node
slides.notes: Two ways in. Point at the table: the cookie changes at every start; rpcauth stays but never stores the password. Ask which suits a program that cannot read the data directory: rpcauth. A common mistake is to paste the password itself into the configuration.
slides.take: The cookie changes at every start; rpcauth is fixed but keeps no password

slides.title: Reading getblockchaininfo
slides.sub: Getting Information on Bitcoin Core's Status
slides.take: Think of a car dashboard: it reports, and you do not touch the engine
slides.notes: This is the answer of a real node of release 31.1 that knew only the first block. Point at blocks 0 and the initial download flag, True. Ask what a fresh node knows: only the first block. A common mistake is to read difficulty 1 as a malfunction.

slides.title: Two status calls, side by side
slides.sub: getblockchaininfo and getnetworkinfo
slides.notes: Two calls report two different things. Point at the left card: the chain, the blocks, the difficulty, the initial download flag. Point at the right card: the node's own version, connections and fees. Ask which call shows if the node is still catching up: getblockchaininfo.
slides.take: One call reports the chain, the other the node's own network

slides.title: Exploring and Decoding Transactions
slides.sub: Reading a transaction the way the node reports it

items.meaning: The hash that names a transaction.
items.analogy: Think of the tracking number on a parcel.

items.meaning: Changing a transaction's id without changing what it does.
items.analogy: Think of a receipt whose number changes when the clerk re-signs it.

items.meaning: The measure by which a block is filled.
items.analogy: Think of postage by volume, where compact data costs less.

slides.notes: Part 5 reads a transaction the way the node reports it. Point at the three tiles: the identifier, malleability and weight. Ask which one is a name and which one is a size. A common mistake is to treat a txid as the transaction itself.

slides.title: A lambda is a function without a name
slides.sub: The one-line helper that the next code uses
slides.notes: A lambda is a function without a name. Point at the four tiles: the keyword, the input, the colon and the returned value. Ask what sat(0.0002) gives: 20,000: the next code box uses exactly this. A common mistake is to think the name sat belongs to the function.
slides.take: A lambda is a tiny function written where it is needed

slides.title: Decoding Alice's transaction
slides.sub: Exploring and Decoding Transactions
slides.take: Think of an X-ray: the same body, shown layer by layer
slides.notes: The node's decoder turns Alice's bytes into fields. Point at the lambda in the first code box and at the two outputs, 20,000 and 75,000 satoshis. Ask where the 5,000 fee is: it is the difference, not a field. A common mistake is to read bitcoin amounts as satoshis.

slides.title: From bytes to fields
slides.sub: Serialization and decoding of Alice's 194 bytes
slides.notes: Serialization writes the bytes; decoding reads them as fields. Point at the coloured strip: version 4, marker and flag 2, inputs 42, outputs 75, witness 67, lock time 4. Ask whether the bytes add up: they add to 194. A common mistake is to forget the marker and flag.
slides.take: Decoding only reads the same bytes in labelled groups

slides.title: The txid leaves the witness out
slides.sub: The transaction ID and transaction malleability
slides.take: Think of a tracking number printed before anyone adds a signature
slides.notes: The txid hashes the transaction without its witness, so a third party can no longer change it. Point at the two different hashes. Ask which one changes if the signature changes: the second. A common mistake is to think the witness is secret: it is only separated.

slides.title: Weight units and virtual bytes
slides.sub: How much of a block a transaction fills
slides.take: Think of postage by volume: compact, light data costs less
slides.notes: Blocks are filled by weight units. Point at the three numbers: 125 base bytes, 69 witness bytes, 569 units. Ask why the virtual size is 143: weight divided by four, rounded up. A common mistake is to add 125 and 69 and call it the weight.

slides.title: Segregated witness and the two identifiers
slides.sub: Why the txid ignores signatures and how weight counts them
slides.notes: Segregated witness moves signatures out of what the txid covers. Point at the three bars: 776 would be the weight with no discount, 569 is the real one. Ask why the txid stays stable: it ignores the witness. A common mistake is to think the witness is thrown away.
slides.take: Moving the signature out gives a stable txid and cheaper block space

slides.title: Exploring Blocks
slides.sub: Height, hash, merkle root and time

items.meaning: A block's place in the chain, counted from zero.
items.analogy: Think of a page number in a very long book.

items.meaning: The name of a block, made by hashing its header.
items.analogy: Think of a fingerprint taken from the page's header.

items.meaning: The middle timestamp of the last eleven blocks.
items.analogy: Think of a median price that one odd sale cannot move.

slides.notes: Part 6 reads blocks. Point at the three tiles: height, hash and median time, and at the table of meanings. Ask which of them one cannot fake: the hash, because it comes from the header. A common mistake is to confuse height with confirmations.

slides.title: Height, depth and confirmations
slides.sub: Example numbers: block 123,456 with five blocks on top
slides.take: A confirmation is one more block on top of yours
slides.notes: Height counts the blocks before a block, so the first has height zero. Point at the row: the tip has one confirmation, itself. Ask how many confirmations block 123,456 has with five on top: six. Students often forget to count their own block.

slides.title: A block's name is the hash of its header
slides.sub: The block hash and the block height of block 123,456
slides.take: Think of a fingerprint taken from the page's header line
slides.notes: The header has six fields in 80 bytes. Point at the sizes: 4, 32, 32, 4, 4, 4. Ask why the hash starts with so many zeros: because proof of work demanded it. A common mistake is to hash the whole block instead of the header, and to forget the reversal.

slides.title: Rebuilding the merkle root
slides.sub: One hash that commits to every transaction of the block
slides.take: Think of a tournament bracket: pairs play, winners meet, one champion remains
slides.notes: Block 123,456 holds 13 transactions. Point at the chart: 13, 7, 4, 2, 1 hashes. Ask what happens at an odd level: the last hash is paired with itself. One changed transaction changes the root; a common mistake is to think the root lists the transactions.

slides.title: Median time of the last eleven blocks
slides.sub: Block timestamps are guesses; the median time is not
slides.take: Think of a median price that one odd sale cannot move
slides.notes: Miners write the time into every header, and it can be a little off. Point at the teal bar, the sixth of eleven sorted times. Ask why a median beats an average: one odd time cannot move it: this is the median time past that the rules use as a clock.

slides.title: Block weight and the block subsidy
slides.sub: How full a block may be, and what its miner may claim
slides.notes: Two limits shape the chain. Point at the chart: the subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25. Ask what it is at block 775,072: 6.25 bitcoins: block weight is the other limit: four million weight units. A common mistake is to read subsidy as the fee.
slides.take: Weight limits the block; halving limits the new coins

slides.title: From the bits field to chain work
slides.sub: How a compact number becomes a target and a count of hashes
slides.notes: Bits is a compact way to write the target. Point at the four steps from the left: bits, length and digits, the shift, then the work. Ask which way the target moves when difficulty rises: down: a smaller target needs more hashes: work is the expected number of hashes.
slides.take: A smaller target means more work, and the most work wins

slides.title: Forks, the best chain and reorganization
slides.sub: What a node does when two branches compete
slides.notes: A fork is two branches. Point at the teal branch: it has more work, so it is the best chain. Ask what happens to the transactions on the orange branch: they return to the mempool unless the teal chain includes them. A common mistake is to count blocks instead of work.
slides.take: The chain with the most work is the best chain

slides.title: Alternative Clients, Libraries, and Toolkits
slides.sub: Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface

items.meaning: A Python library that calls the node and builds transactions.
items.analogy: Think of a phrasebook that turns your Python into the node's language.

items.meaning: Another program that follows Bitcoin's rules.
items.analogy: Think of another airline flying the same routes under the same safety rules.

slides.notes: Part 7 looks beyond Bitcoin Core. Point at the two tiles: a library that calls the node, and other clients. Ask which language students would pick for a first script. A common mistake is to assume every client agrees with Core on every rule.

slides.title: Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface
slides.sub: python-bitcoinlib calls the node for you
slides.take: Your code can ask the node anything the command line can
slides.notes: A library speaks to the node for you. Point at the four boxes: script, library, HTTP, node. Ask where the JSON-RPC call is built: in the library. On the offline node of release 31.1 a call for the block count returned zero, as the card says.

slides.title: Libraries, wrappers and registries
slides.sub: Where toolkits live and how they reach the node
slides.notes: A wrapper library hides the HTTP call. Point at the stack: your program, the library, JSON-RPC, the node. Then point at the registry card: it lists libraries with versions and release dates. Ask where to check a library's age: in the registry: old is not the same as useless.
slides.take: A wrapper hides the HTTP call; a registry shows how fresh a library is

slides.title: How fresh are the alternative toolkits
slides.sub: python-bitcoinlib and its neighbours, by days since the latest release
slides.take: Think of the date on the newest delivery in a shop window
slides.notes: Toolkits age. Point at the log scale: 25 days against 1,217 days. Ask which library a student would trust for a new project, and why. A common mistake is to read the bar height on a log axis as a simple ratio.

slides.title: Facts with a name: verified and linked data
slides.sub: Your own node's answers, and how JSON becomes linked data
slides.notes: Data from your own node is authoritative because the node verified it. Point at the three columns: plain JSON, the context, the IRI names. Ask what a context changes: not the shape, only the meaning of the keys: the example.org names are illustrations, not a real vocabulary.
slides.take: A context turns plain JSON keys into global names

slides.title: Computing words, part one: numbers
slides.sub: Four small ideas under the numbers of this chapter
slides.notes: Four small ideas carry the numbers of this chapter. Point at the third column: each one has a place on an earlier slide. Ask who can find the bit shift in the version-bits example. A common mistake is to treat a byte as one hexadecimal digit; it is two.
slides.take: Plain computing ideas carry the numbers

slides.title: Computing words, part two: systems
slides.sub: Seven words from computing and where they appear
slides.notes: Seven words from computing sit under the chapter. Point at the second column: where each one appears. Ask which one a student met in the build and which in the node. A common mistake is to confuse a process with a thread, or a library with a program.
slides.take: The words of computing name the parts of a node

slides.title: Summary: the six answers
slides.take: Reference, release, settings, interface, transaction, block
slides.notes: Each row answers one of the six opening questions. Point at the first words of each answer and ask students to answer in their own words, using the everyday pictures. A common mistake is to memorise the table instead of one answer for each question.

slides.take: Build a release, run it offline, and ask it getblockchaininfo
slides.notes: These links are all open and free. Point at the chapter source and the release page first, then the RPC reference. Ask which link a student will open tonight. Community links are where questions get answered; the talk on tracing a running node is a good evening watch.

slides.title: Questions?
slides.notes: That is Bitcoin Core from source to answers. Chapter 4 turns to keys and addresses, which the node's wallet depends on. Ask for one question per student before they leave, and write them on the board for the start of the next lecture.
